title: Solids: Surface Area and Volume
tagline: Surface area and volume of cylinder, cone, and sphere, including combined solids and unit conversions.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class X Mathematics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every numerical result in this chapter was independently recomputed. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: This chapter extends plane geometry to three-dimensional solids. Students learn to compute the surface area and volume of the right circular cylinder, right circular cone, and sphere, as well as combinations of these solids (such as a cylinder with a conical top, or a hemisphere surmounted on a cube). The chapter also covers unit conversions (between cm³, m³, litres, and millilitres) and applies these concepts to real-world problems involving capacity, materials, and packaging.

learningOutcomes: State the formulae for the volume and surface area of a cylinder, cone, and sphere (including hemisphere).
Apply the formulae to find unknown radii, heights, or slant heights when two of the three quantities are given.
Solve problems involving combined solids (e.g., a cone on top of a cylinder, a hemisphere inside a cylinder, a sphere with a cylindrical hole).
Convert between volume units: cm³, m³, 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³, 1 litre = 1000 cm³, 1 m³ = 1000 litres.
Solve real-world problems involving capacity, material costs, and packaging.
Verify that formulae are applied correctly by checking dimensions and reasonableness of the answer.

blocks.text: Three-dimensional solids occupy space and have two measures: surface area (the total area of the outer surface) and volume (the amount of space enclosed). The solids studied in ICSE Class X are the cylinder, the cone, and the sphere (including its hemisphere). Each solid has specific formulae that must be applied correctly, paying attention to whether the problem asks for curved surface area, total surface area, or volume. The radius (r) is the distance from the centre to the curved surface; the height (h) is the perpendicular distance between the bases (for cylinder and cone); the slant height (l) is the distance from the vertex to a point on the base edge (for cone); and the diameter is twice the radius.

Labels on a cylinder: r (radius), h (height), 2h (curved height), l (slant height, applicable to cone). Labels on a cone: r (radius), h (vertical height), l (slant height). Labels on a sphere: r (radius). Labels on a hemisphere: r (radius), curved surface vs. total surface.

items: π ≈ 3.14 or 22/7, unless otherwise stated.
For the cone, l = √(r² + h²) (Pythagoras' theorem) when the slant height is not given.
Hemisphere is half a sphere; its total surface area includes the flat circular base (πr²) plus the curved surface (2πr²).
Always identify whether the problem asks for curved surface area or total surface area before applying the formula.

blocks.text: A right circular cylinder has a circular base and a perpendicular height. If the radius of the base is r and the height is h, then: Volume V = πr²h (the area of the base times the height). Curved Surface Area CSA = 2πrh (the area of the side surface, excluding the top and bottom). Total Surface Area TSA = 2πr(r + h) = 2πrh + 2πr² (the curved surface plus the top and bottom circles).

items.text: Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 5 cm and height 10 cm.
Find the total surface area of a cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 7 cm.
A cylindrical water tank has radius 2 m and height 1.5 m. How many litres of water can it hold?
items.note: Volume = π × 2² × 1.5 = 6π m³ ≈ 18.84 m³. In litres: 18.84 × 1000 = 18,840 litres. V = πr²h = π × 2² × 1.5 = 6π m³. Since 1 m³ = 1000 litres, the capacity is 6π × 1000 ≈ 18,840 litres.

items: When finding the volume, always use the perpendicular height, not the slant height.
Curved surface area excludes the top and bottom bases; total surface area includes them.
Unit conversions: 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³, 1 litre = 1000 cm³, 1 m³ = 1000 litres.
π may be taken as 22/7 or 3.14, unless the problem specifies otherwise.

blocks.text: A right circular cone has a circular base and a vertex (apex) directly above the centre of the base. If the radius of the base is r, the vertical height is h, and the slant height is l, then: Volume V = (1/3)πr²h (one-third of the cylinder with the same base and height). Curved Surface Area CSA = πrl. Total Surface Area TSA = πr(r + l) = πr² + πrl (the base circle plus the curved surface). The slant height l is found from r and h using Pythagoras: l = √(r² + h²).

items.text: Find the volume of a cone with radius 6 cm and height 8 cm.
items.note: First, l = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 cm. Then V = (1/3)π × 6² × 8 = (1/3)π × 36 × 8 = 96π cm³ ≈ 301.6 cm³. V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π × 36 × 8 = 96π. The slant height is found via Pythagoras as a subsidiary step.

items.text: Find the total surface area of a cone with radius 4 cm and slant height 5 cm.
A conical tent has a base radius of 3 m and a height of 4 m. Find the curved surface area of the canvas needed.
items.note: First, l = √(3² + 4²) = 5 m. Then CSA = π × 3 × 5 = 15π m² ≈ 47.1 m². l = √(r² + h²) = √(9 + 16) = 5. CSA = πrl = π × 3 × 5 = 15π.

items: Always find the slant height l = √(r² + h²) when it is not given.
The volume of a cone is one-third the volume of a cylinder with the same base and height.
Total surface area includes the base; curved surface area excludes it.
When a cone is combined with another solid, identify which faces are exposed and which are hidden.

learn.title: Sphere and Hemisphere: Formulae and Calculations

blocks.text: A sphere is the set of all points in space at a fixed distance (radius r) from a centre point. A hemisphere is half a sphere, cut through the centre. The sphere has no flat faces; the hemisphere has a flat circular base (area πr²) and a curved surface (area 2πr²). Formulae: Sphere volume V = (4/3)πr³, Sphere surface area SA = 4πr². Hemisphere volume V = (2/3)πr³, Hemisphere total surface area TSA = πr² (base) + 2πr² (curved) = 3πr², Hemisphere curved surface area CSA = 2πr².

items.text: Find the surface area of a sphere with radius 7 cm.
Find the volume of a hemisphere with radius 3 cm.
A hemispherical bowl of radius 5 cm is filled with water. How many millilitres of water does it hold? (1 cm³ = 1 mL)
items.note: V = (2/3)π × 5³ = (2/3)π × 125 = 250π/3 cm³ ≈ 261.8 mL. V = (2/3)πr³ = (2/3)π × 125 = 250π/3 cm³. Since 1 cm³ = 1 mL, the capacity is 250π/3 mL ≈ 261.8 mL.

items: The hemisphere total surface area includes the flat circular base (area πr²) plus the curved surface (area 2πr²).
Curved surface area of a hemisphere is half the sphere's surface area: 2πr².
Unit conversions: 1 cm³ = 1 mL. 1 litre = 1000 cm³.
When a hemisphere is surmounted on a cube or cylinder, the base of the hemisphere coincides with the top face of the other solid, so the exposed area excludes the base.

blocks.text: Many ICSE Class X problems involve combinations of two or more solids, such as a cylinder with a conical top, a hemisphere surmounted on a cube, or a sphere with a cylindrical hole. The key principle is: (1) Compute the surface area or volume of each component separately, then (2) add or subtract as needed, taking care to exclude any faces that are internal (not exposed). For surface area: add the exposed curved surfaces; do NOT add the areas of internal flat faces that are joined together. For volume: add the volumes of the component solids (if the combined solid is the union) or subtract the volume of the removed portion (if the combined solid is the difference).

items.text: A solid consists of a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 10 cm, with a cone of radius 3 cm and height 4 cm on top. Find the total surface area.
items.note: Cylinder CSA = 2πrh = 2π × 3 × 10 = 60π. Cone CSA = πrl, where l = √(3² + 4²) = 5, so CSA = π × 3 × 5 = 15π. The cylinder's top base is covered by the cone's base, so it is not exposed. The cylinder's bottom base IS exposed: area = πr² = 9π. Total TSA = 60π + 15π + 9π = 84π cm² ≈ 263.9 cm². The total surface area consists of the cylinder's curved surface (60π), the cone's curved surface (15π), and the cylinder's bottom base (9π). The cylinder's top base and the cone's base are joined together and are not exposed.

items.text: A cube of side 6 cm has a hemisphere of radius 3 cm surmounted on its top face. Find the total surface area of the resulting solid.
items.note: Cube TSA without top face = 5 × 6² = 180 cm² (five faces exposed, the top is covered by the hemisphere). Hemisphere curved surface = 2πr² = 2π × 3² = 18π. The hemisphere's flat base coincides with the cube's top face and is not added again. Total TSA = 180 + 18π cm² ≈ 236.5 cm². The cube has 5 exposed faces (the top face is covered by the hemisphere). The hemisphere contributes its curved surface area only; its flat base is internal and not counted.

items.text: A cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 12 cm has a conical hole of radius 4 cm and slant height 5 cm drilled through it. Find the volume of the remaining solid.
items.note: Cylinder volume = πr²h = π × 4² × 12 = 192π cm³. Cone volume = (1/3)πr²h, where h = √(l² − r²) = √(25 − 16) = 3, so cone volume = (1/3)π × 16 × 3 = 16π cm³. Remaining volume = 192π − 16π = 176π cm³ ≈ 552.9 cm³. The volume of the remaining solid is the cylinder volume minus the volume of the conical hole. The cone's vertical height is found via Pythagoras: h = √(l² − r²) = √(25 − 16) = 3 cm.

items: For surface area: add only the exposed curved surfaces; exclude internal flat faces that are joined.
For volume: add the volumes of component solids (union) or subtract the removed portion (difference).
When a cone sits on a cylinder, the top base of the cylinder is not exposed.
When a hemisphere sits on a cube or cylinder, the flat base of the hemisphere is not exposed.
Always identify which faces/areas are internal and should be excluded.

blocks.text: Solid geometry problems often require converting between volume units. The key conversions are: 1 m = 100 cm, 1 m² = 10,000 cm², 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³ (10⁶ cm³), 1 litre = 1000 cm³, and 1 m³ = 1000 litres. When converting, cube the linear conversion factor.

items.text: A cylindrical tank of capacity 2 m³ is filled with water. How many litres of water is this?
items.note: 2 m³ = 2 × 1000 = 2000 litres. Since 1 m³ = 1000 litres, 2 m³ = 2000 litres.

items.text: A tank holds 250 litres of water. Express this in m³.
items.note: 250 litres = 250 / 1000 = 0.25 m³. Since 1 m³ = 1000 litres, divide by 1000.

items: 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³ (cube the factor 100).
1 litre = 1000 cm³.
1 m³ = 1000 litres.
Always check that the conversion factor is applied correctly (multiply or divide).

blocks.text: The questions that follow move from straightforward formula applications through multi-step problems involving combined solids and unit conversions to reasoning about which faces are exposed. Work each one by identifying the solid(s), writing the relevant formula, and substituting the given values.

keyPoints: For a cylinder of radius r and height h: volume V = πr²h, curved surface area = 2πrh, and total surface area = 2πr(h + r).
For a cone of radius r, vertical height h and slant height l: volume V = (1/3)πr²h, curved surface area = πrl, and total surface area = πr(r + l).
The slant height of a cone comes from Pythagoras, l = √(r² + h²), and is never the same as the vertical height h.
For a sphere of radius r: volume V = (4/3)πr³ and surface area = 4πr²; a hemisphere has half the volume, curved area 2πr² and total area 3πr².
Melting and recasting conserve volume: the original solid's volume equals the sum of the volumes of the new pieces, never their surface areas.
Lengths, areas and volumes scale by the scale factor, its square and its cube: doubling every length of a solid multiplies its surface area by 4 and its volume by 8.
Capacity conversions: 1 litre = 1000 cm³ and 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³ = 1000 litres.
For a combined solid, list every exposed face before adding areas; the circle where two parts meet is internal and belongs to neither surface.
examFocus: Write the radius, the height and the value of π in use at the top of the working before substituting into any formula, and keep one formula per line.
Architecture questions about melting and recasting are volume-conservation questions: compute the original volume, divide by one new piece, and only then round the count to a whole number.
A question that gives the slant height expects πrl immediately; one that gives the vertical height expects Pythagoras first. Marking which was given avoids the most common lost mark.
For a combined solid, exactly two things are asked in most papers: the total surface area of the exposed faces and the volume of the whole. Beware of the joined face in the area part.
Answers involving litres must carry the cm³-to-litre conversion explicitly; silently dividing by 1000 loses the method mark even when the number is right.

vocabulary.meaning: The distance along the curved face of a cone from a point on the base circle to the apex; found with Pythagoras from the radius and the vertical height.
The area of the lateral face only — 2πrh for a cylinder, πrl for a cone, 2πr² for a hemisphere — excluding any flat circular faces.
The area of every exposed face of a solid, curved faces and flat circles together.
Half of a sphere cut by a plane through its centre; its volume is (2/3)πr³ and its flat face is a circle of area πr².
The volume a hollow vessel can hold, usually quoted in litres where 1 litre = 1000 cm³.
Melting a solid and reforming the metal into new shapes; the total volume is unchanged by the process.
A solid made of two or more standard solids joined, for which volumes are added but the meeting face is excluded from surface areas.
The reverse of cubing; the edge of a cube of volume 216 cm³ is ∛216 = 6 cm, used whenever volumes are scaled.

questions.prompt: The curved surface area of a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm is:
questions.explanation: The curved surface area is 2πrh = 2 x (22/7) x 7 x 10 = 440 cm², since the radius 7 cancels the 7 in π = 22/7.
questions.commonMistake: Using πr² h (the volume formula) instead of 2πrh, which gives 1540 cm³ and does not match any curved-area option.

questions.prompt: The volume of a cone of base radius 6 cm and height 7 cm is:
questions.explanation: V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3) x (22/7) x 36 x 7 = (1/3) x 36 x 22 = 264 cm³; the factor 7 cancels and the 1/3 divides 36 into 12.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting the factor 1/3, which gives the cylinder volume 792 cm³ instead of the cone volume.

questions.prompt: The surface area of a sphere of radius 7 cm is:
questions.explanation: The surface area of a sphere is 4πr² = 4 x (22/7) x 49 = 4 x 22 x 7 = 616 cm².
questions.commonMistake: Using 2πr² (twice the base circle instead of four times it), which gives 308 cm².

questions.prompt: The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm is:
questions.explanation: A solid hemisphere has a curved face of 2πr² and a flat circular face of πr², so the total is 3πr² = 3 x (22/7) x 49 = 462 cm².
questions.commonMistake: Adding the flat circle twice (or omitting it entirely), which gives 616 cm² or 308 cm² instead of 462 cm².

questions.prompt: A sphere has the same radius as a cylinder whose height equals the sphere's diameter. The ratio of the volume of the sphere to the volume of the cylinder is:
questions.explanation: The cylinder has radius r and height 2r, so its volume is 2πr³, while the sphere's volume is (4/3)πr³. The ratio is (4/3) : 2 = 2 : 3 after multiplying both sides by 3.
questions.commonMistake: Comparing the sphere with a cylinder of height r rather than 2r, which gives the familiar but here irrelevant 2 : 1 ratio.

questions.prompt: A cylinder and a cone have the same base radius and the same height. The volume of the cylinder exceeds the volume of the cube of the cone's radius by how many times the cone's volume?
questions.explanation: V_cylinder = πr²h and V_cone = (1/3)πr²h, so the cylinder holds exactly three times the cone; the difference is two cones' worth of volume.
questions.commonMistake: Reporting the cylinder/cone ratio as the difference between x2 and x3 factors of other pairs of solids, forgetting that the 1/3 in the cone formula is exact.

questions.prompt: If the diameter of a cylinder is doubled while its height stays the same, its curved surface area becomes:
questions.explanation: CSA = 2πrh depends linearly on r. Doubling the diameter doubles r and therefore doubles the curved surface area.
questions.commonMistake: Squaring the scale factor as though the area depended on r², which would be true for the circular ends but not for the 2πrh term.

questions.prompt: If the radius of a sphere increases by 10 per cent, its volume increases by approximately:
questions.explanation: Volume depends on r³, so the scale factor is 1.1³ = 1.331, an increase of 33.1 per cent; the 10 per cent radius rise compounds through the three factors of r.
questions.commonMistake: Adding 10 per cent three times to reach 30 per cent, which ignores the compounding (cubic) dependence of volume on radius.

questions.prompt: The total surface area of a cylinder of radius r and height h is 2πr(____ + r).
questions.explanation: The total surface area adds the curved face 2πrh to the two circular ends, which together are 2πr², so it factors as 2πr(h + r); the missing quantity in the bracket is the height h.
questions.commonMistake: Writing h/2 or 2h, which breaks the factorisation that pairs one 2 with h for the curved face and one r with π for an end.

questions.prompt: The volume of a hemisphere is exactly ____ the volume of the sphere with the same radius.
questions.explanation: Cutting a sphere in half by a plane through its centre produces two identical hemispheres, each carrying (1/2) x (4/3)πr³ = (2/3)πr³ of volume.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing volume with surface area, where the hemisphere has two-thirds of the sphere's area plus a flat circle rather than a fixed half.

questions.prompt: 1 litre equals ____ cubic centimetres.
questions.explanation: A litre is defined as a cube 10 cm on a side, and 10³ = 1000, so capacity conversions move between litres and cm³ with a factor of exactly 1000.
questions.commonMistake: Dividing by 100 instead of 1000 because cm-to-metre conversions use 100; capacity uses the cube of 10, not 10.

questions.prompt: The volume of a cone equals ____ of the volume of the cylinder with the same base and the same height.
questions.explanation: V_cone = (1/3)πr²h against V_cylinder = πr²h shows the cone fills exactly one third of the cylinder; three full cones refill one cylinder.
questions.commonMistake: Using two thirds, which is the hemisphere-to-sphere ratio rather than the cone-to-cylinder ratio.

questions.prompt: The total surface area of a cube of edge 5 cm is ____.
questions.explanation: A cube has six square faces each of area 5² = 25 cm², so the total surface area is 6 x 25 = 150 cm².
questions.commonMistake: Reporting 25 cm², which is the area of a single face rather than all six.

questions.prompt: A closed cylindrical tin of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm is made of sheet metal. Find its total surface area.
questions.explanation: The curved surface is 2πrh = 2 x (22/7) x 7 x 10 = 440 cm². The two ends contribute 2πr² = 2 x (22/7) x 49 = 308 cm². The total is 440 + 308 = 748 cm², which also equals 2πr(h + r) = 2 x (22/7) x 7 x 17 = 748 cm².
questions.commonMistake: Counting only one circular end, or multiplying 440 by 3/2 rather than adding the exact 308 cm² of the two ends.

questions.prompt: A right circular cone has base radius 8 cm and vertical height 15 cm. Find its slant height.
questions.explanation: The slant height is the hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by the radius and the vertical height: l = √(r² + h²) = √(64 + 225) = √289 = 17 cm.
questions.commonMistake: Adding r and h linearly (8 + 15 = 23) instead of applying Pythagoras' theorem.

questions.prompt: A hemispherical bowl has an internal radius of 21 cm. Find its capacity in litres.
questions.explanation: The capacity is the hemisphere volume (2/3)πr³ = (2/3) x (22/7) x 21³. Since 21³ = 9261 and 9261/21 = 441, the volume is (2 x 22 x 441) x 21/21 = 44 x 441 = 19404 cm³. Dividing by 1000 converts to 19.404 litres.
questions.commonMistake: Using the sphere volume 4πr³/3, which doubles the answer to 38.808 litres, or forgetting the cm³-to-litre division.

questions.prompt: A spherical ball of radius 4.2 cm is melted and recast into 8 identical smaller balls. Find the radius of each smaller ball.
questions.explanation: Eight small balls carry eight times the volume of one small ball equal to the original, so each small ball has one eighth of the original volume. Volumes scale as the cube of the radius, so the radius scales by the cube root of 1/8 = 1/2, giving 4.2 / 2 = 2.1 cm.
questions.commonMistake: Halving the volume and then reporting the radius as half of 2.1 cm, which treats the radius as though it scaled linearly with volume.

questions.prompt: A solid metal sphere of radius 7 cm is melted and recast into identical small cones, each of base radius 7 cm and height 4 cm. How many cones are formed?
questions.explanation: The sphere has volume (4/3)πr³ = (4/3)π x 343 = 1372π/3. Each cone has volume (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π x 49 x 4 = 196π/3. Dividing, (1372π/3) / (196π/3) = 1372/196 = 7, so exactly 7 cones are formed with no metal wasted.
questions.commonMistake: Comparing surface areas rather than volumes when counting the recast pieces; melting conserves volume, not surface area.

questions.prompt: A solid toy is made from a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm with a solid hemisphere mounted on one flat face (the same radius). Taking π = 22/7, find (i) the total surface area of the toy and (ii) its volume.
questions.answer: Total surface area 902 cm²; volume 2258 2/3 cm³ (about 2258.67 cm³)
questions.explanation: The exposed faces are the cylinder's curved surface, the cylinder's bottom circle, and the hemisphere's curved surface: 2πrh + πr² + 2πr² = 2 x (22/7) x 7 x 10 + (22/7) x 49 x 3 = 440 + 462 = 902 cm². The volume is the cylinder plus the hemisphere: πr²h + (2/3)πr³ = (22/7) x 49 x 10 + (2/3) x (22/7) x 343 = 1540 + 2156/3 = 6776/3 = 2258 2/3 cm³, that is about 2258.67 cm³.
questions.commonMistake: Including the contact circle twice, or subtracting the hemisphere's flat face from the mounted cylinder without checking which faces are actually exposed.

questions.prompt: A solid sphere of radius 6 cm is fully submerged in a cylindrical jar of internal radius 6 cm that already contains water. Find the rise in the water level.
questions.explanation: The displaced volume equals the sphere volume (4/3)πr³. It spreads through the jar of base area πr² (same radius), so the rise is (4/3)πr³ / πr² = (4/3)r = (4/3) x 6 = 8 cm.
questions.commonMistake: Using the jar's diameter rather than its radius as the base dimension, which halves the base area and doubles the computed rise to 16 cm.

questions.prompt: Water from a full conical vessel of base radius 6 cm and height 21 cm is emptied into an empty cylindrical glass of base radius 3 cm. How deep does the water stand in the glass?
questions.explanation: The cone holds (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π x 36 x 21 = 252π cm³. In the cylinder the same volume stands as πR² x depth = 9π x depth, so the depth is 252π / 9π = 28 cm. The π cancels, so the answer is exact.
questions.commonMistake: Equating heights instead of volumes (28 would then have to come from 21 x 4/3 without justifying the 4/3), rather than dividing the cone volume by the glass base area.

questions.prompt: Three metallic cubes of edges 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm are melted together into a single cube. Find the edge of the new cube and verify it by computing both the sum of the three volumes and the new cube's volume.
questions.explanation: The three volumes are 3³ = 27, 4³ = 64 and 5³ = 125 cm³, summing to 216 cm³. The new cube therefore has edge ∛216 = 6 cm, and 6³ = 216 cm³ confirms the conservation of volume.
questions.commonMistake: Adding the edges (3 + 4 + 5 = 12) instead of the volumes, which would give an edge of 12 cm and eight times the original material.

questions.prompt: A solid cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 63 cm is melted and recast into identical spheres of radius 3.5 cm each. How many spheres are formed?
questions.explanation: The cylinder volume is πr²h = π x 49 x 63 = 3087π. Each sphere has volume (4/3)π r³ = (4/3)π x 42.875 = 57.1666...,π. Dividing: 3087π / ((4/3) x 42.875π) = (49 x 63) / ((4/3) x (7/2)³). Working with fractions: (4/3) x (343/8) = 343/6, so the count is 3087 / (343/6) = 3087 x 6 / 343 = 9 x 6 / 1 x 343/343 = 54 spheres exactly.
questions.commonMistake: Rounding the volume of one sphere to 57.17 cm³ and then dividing 3087π to get 53.99, then rounding to 53; keeping exact fractions shows the count is exactly 54.
